Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TMicro services Architecture: Introduction Concept
Introduction
•Microservices Architecture (MSA)  is a software architectural style  where an application is 
structured as a collection of small, loosely coupled, independently deployable services . •Each service is designed to perform a single business function  and communicates with 
other services using lightweight protocols (typically HTTP/REST or gRPC , sometimes 
messaging queues like Kafka/RabbitMQ). •It contrasts with the monolithic architecture , where all modules and components are 
tightly integrated into one large application.

heading: Page 6
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TMicro services Architecture: Introduction Concept
Key Concepts
•Independence  – Each microservice can be developed, deployed, and scaled 
independently. •Single Responsibility Principle  – A service is designed around one business capability 
(e.g., Payment Service, Inventory Service, User Authentication Service ). •Technology Agnostic  – Different microservices can be built using different programming 
languages or databases as long as they follow agreed communication protocols (polyglot 
persistence). •Decentralized Data Management  – Each service manages its own database/schema to 
avoid tight coupling. •Communication  – Services interact using APIs, event -driven messaging, or service meshes. •Resilience & Fault Tolerance  – Failure in one service should not crash the whole system. •Scalability  – Services can be scaled horizontally (individually) based on demand.

heading: Page 7
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TMicro services Architecture: Introduction Concept
Advantages
•Faster development and deployment cycles. •Easier to adopt DevOps & CI/CD pipelines . •Independent scaling reduces infrastructure costs. •Improved fault isolation. •Flexibility in technology choices. •Easier to maintain and update specific parts of the application. Challenges
•Complexity in design and management.

heading: Page 7
text: •Requires advanced orchestration tools  (e.g., Kubernetes, Docker Swarm). •Data consistency can be challenging (eventual consistency). •Monitoring, logging, and debugging become harder. •Higher communication overhead compared to monoliths.

Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TDomain Driven Design
Introduction
•Domain -Driven Design (DDD) is a software design approach introduced by Eric Evans. It 
focuses on building software around the business domain instead of only the technical 
implementation. •The idea: Instead of just focusing on technology, software should be modeled around 
business problems and concepts . •It’s especially relevant in cloud -native and microservices environments , where aligning 
services to business capabilities is crucial.

Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TDomain Driven Design
Core Concepts of DDD
•Domain: The sphere of knowledge, activity, or interest around which the application logic revolves 
(e.g., banking, healthcare, e -commerce). •Model: An abstraction that describes selected aspects of the domain and helps solve problems. •Ubiquitous Language: A common vocabulary used consistently by developers, domain experts, 
and stakeholders to reduce miscommunication. •Bounded Context: A logical boundary where a particular domain model is defined and applicable. •Example: In e-commerce, “Order Management” and “Inventory Management” are separate 
bounded contexts. Both use the word “Product”, but in different ways.

heading: Page 12
text:
•Entities: Objects that have an identity and persist over time (e.g., Customer name ). •Value Objects: Objects that are immutable and defined by their values; no identity (e.g., Address ). •Aggregates: A cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit (root entity + value objects). •Repositories: Mechanisms for retrieving and storing domain objects. •Domain Events: Events that capture things that happened in the domain (e.g., OrderPlaced , 
PaymentProcessed ).

•Aligns software closely with business requirements. •Reduces miscommunication between developers & domain experts.

Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TModelling: Bounded Context
Introduction
•Bounded Context  is one of the central patterns in Domain -Driven Design (DDD) . •A bounded context  defines a clear boundary within which a particular domain model is 
valid and consistent . •Inside this boundary:
•Terms, concepts, and rules have a specific meaning . •Outside this boundary, the same term may have a different meaning . •It prevents ambiguity and model conflicts  when multiple teams work on large systems. Example: 
In an e-commerce platform :
•“Order”  in the Order Management context  means a customer’s purchase. •“Order”  in the Inventory context  might mean a supplier restock order.

heading: Page 16
text: •Same word, different meaning → hence separate bounded contexts .

heading: Page 17
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TModelling: Bounded Context
Why Bounded Contexts are Important
•Large systems have multiple sub-domains  (e.g., payments, shipping, inventory). •Without clear boundaries, the model becomes inconsistent and complex. •Bounded Context ensures model clarity, team autonomy, and scalability . •In cloud -native microservices , bounded contexts map directly to microservices 
boundaries . Core Principles
•Explicit Boundaries  – Defines what’s inside and outside the context. •Ubiquitous Language within Context  – Terms have one meaning within a context. •Context Mapping  – Shows how multiple bounded contexts relate to each other (shared 
kernel, customer -supplier, anti -corruption layer). •Autonomy  – Each context evolves independently.

heading: Page 18
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TModelling: Bounded Context
Advantages
•Prevents domain model confusion. •Simplifies communication between business experts and developers. •Enables team autonomy  (each team owns one bounded context/microservice). •Aligns naturally with microservices architecture . •Improves maintainability and scalability .

heading: Page 18
text:
Challenges
•Requires deep analysis of business processes. •Risk of over -segmentation  if too many contexts are created. •Inter -context communication can become complex. •Needs good documentation and collaboration.

Elements of Microservices Architecture
a) Service
•The smallest unit in microservices. •Performs one task (e.g., Payment service). •Runs independently and communicates with others via APIs. b) API Gateway
•Entry point for all client requests. •Routes requests to the correct service. •Handles security, load balancing, and logging. •Example: Netflix API Gateway.

heading: Page 25
text:
c) Database per Service
•Each microservice can have its own database  (ensures loose coupling). •Example: User Service uses MongoDB, Payment Service uses MySQL.

heading: Page 26
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TElement of micro services and implementation mechanism
d) Service Discovery
•Helps microservices find each other  automatically. •Example: Netflix Eureka, Consul.

heading: Page 26
text:
e) Load Balancer
•Distributes requests evenly across instances of microservices. •Ensures high availability. f) Inter -service Communication
•Microservices communicate using:
Synchronous : REST APIs / gRPC
Asynchronous : Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ). g) Security
•Authentication and authorization between services (OAuth2, JWT). h) Monitoring and Logging
•Essential to track system health and performance. •Tools: Prometheus, ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana).

Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TTechnology: Container - Kubernetes part 2
Advanced Container Concepts
1. Container Networking - Container networking enables containers to communicate with 
each other and with external applications. •Every container gets its own network interface and IP . •Docker supports Bridge, Host, and Overlay networks. •Overlay networks connect containers running on different hosts. Real -time example: In a food delivery app, the Order Service container communicates with 
the Payment Service container through a container network.

heading: Page 32
text:
Volumes and Persistent Storage - Volumes provide persistent storage so data is not lost 
when a container stops or restarts. •Container storage is temporary. •Volumes are stored outside the container. •The same volume can be reused by new containers.

heading: Page 32
text:
Real -time example: Customer order history in a MySQL container remains available even 
after the container restarts.

heading: Page 33
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TTechnology: Container - Kubernetes part 2
3. Environment Variables and Secrets - Configuration values and sensitive information are 
supplied to containers without changing the application code. •Environment variables store configuration such as port number or database URL. •Secrets store passwords, API keys, and authentication tokens. •Makes applications portable across development, testing, and production.

heading: Page 33
text:
Real -time example: The Payment Service receives the Razorpay  API key as a secret instead 
of storing it inside the Docker image. Container Resource Management - Containers can be assigned CPU and memory limits to 
ensure efficient resource usage. •CPU limits prevent one container from consuming all processor resources. •Memory limits prevent excessive RAM usage. •Helps multiple containers run efficiently on the same host. Real -time example: During peak food orders, the Recommendation Service is limited to 1 GB 
RAM so it doesn't affect the Payment Service.

heading: Page 34
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TTechnology: Container - Kubernetes part 2
5. Container Image Optimization - Techniques used to build smaller, faster, and more secure 
container images. •Use lightweight base images (Alpine, Distroless ). •Use multi -stage builds to reduce image size. •Remove unnecessary files and dependencies.

heading: Page 34
text:
Real -time example: Swiggy reduces the Order Service image from 700 MB to 150 MB, 
making deployments much faster. Container Registry - A repository where container images are stored and shared. •Developers push images to a registry. •Servers or Kubernetes pull images from the registry. •Popular registries include Docker Hub, Amazon ECR, Azure ACR, and Google Artifact 
Registry. Real -time example: After developers build a new Food Delivery app image, it is pushed to 
Docker Hub, and Kubernetes downloads the latest version for deployment.

Advanced Kubernetes Concepts
1) Namespaces: A Namespace is a logical partition inside a Kubernetes cluster. It allows 
multiple teams or environments to use the same Kubernetes cluster without interfering 
with each other.

heading: Page 36
text:
Example: College ERP Example
•dev namespace → Developers test attendance application. •test namespace → QA team tests the application. •prod namespace → Students use the live application. 2) ConfigMaps  and Secrets: These store configuration separately from the application. ConfigMap  - Stores non -sensitive configuration data. Examples: Database hostname, Application port, Environment variables, API endpoint URL.

heading: Page 36
text: Secret - Stores sensitive information. Examples: Database password, API keys, JWT tokens, Certificates.

heading: Page 37

3) StatefulSets  - A StatefulSet  manages applications that need persistent identity and 
storage. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Cassandra, Kafka
4) Persistent Volumes (PV) and Persistent Volume Claims (PVC)
•Containers lose data when restarted. •Kubernetes solves this using Persistent Storage. Persistent Volume (PV)
•A storage resource available inside the cluster. •It may come from: Local disk, AWS EBS, Azure Dis, Google Persistent Disk.

heading: Page 37
text:
Persistent Volume Claim (PVC)
•A request made by a Pod asking Kubernetes for storage. Flow
1.Storage exists (PV). 2.Pod requests storage (PVC). 3.Kubernetes attaches storage to Pod.

heading: Page 37
text: Example: MySQL Pod stores student records. Even if the Pod restarts, the database remains.

5) Kubernetes Networking
•Networking allows Pods and users to communicate. •Each Pod gets its own IP . •Services expose Pods using ClusterIP , NodePort , or LoadBalancer .

heading: Page 38
text:
•Ingress Controller  (e.g., NGINX Ingress) manages external access with routing rules. 6) Service Mesh (Istio/ Linkerd )
•A Service Mesh manages communication between microservices. •Instead of adding networking code into applications, the mesh handles it. •Features: Traffic routing, Monitoring, Security, Encryption, Load balancing
•Real -Time Example: Attendance Service communicates with Student Service securely

Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TTechnology: Inter -micro services communication
Introduction
•In a microservices architecture , multiple services work together to form a complete 
application. •Example: In an e -commerce app:
•User Service  (authentication)
•Order Service  (manages orders)
•Payment Service  (processes payments)
•Inventory Service  (stock updates)
•For the system to function, services must communicate  effectively with each other. This is called Inter -Microservices Communication .

heading: Page 41
text: Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TTechnology: Inter -micro services communication

heading: Page 42
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TTechnology: Inter -micro services communication
Types of Inter -Service Communication
a) Synchronous Communication
•One service directly calls another and waits for a response. •Protocols: HTTP/REST, gRPC , GraphQL . •Example: Order Service calls Payment Service → waits for confirmation. Pros : Simple, widely used, direct response. Cons : Tight coupling, failure in one service can affect others. b) Asynchronous Communication
•Services communicate via message brokers  (no waiting). •Protocols: Message Queues, Event Streaming  (Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS SQS). •Example: Order Service places an "Order Created" event → Inventory Service consumes it.

heading: Page 42
text:
•
  Pros : Decoupled, scalable, fault -tolerant. Cons : More complex, requires message management.

heading: Page 43
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TTechnology: Inter -micro services communication
c) Event -Driven Communication
•Services publish events → other services subscribe . •Example: Payment Success → triggers Shipping Service. •Tools: Apache Kafka, NATS, AWS SNS . Real -Time Applications
•Netflix  → Uses gRPC  + event streaming for video recommendations & personalization. •Uber  → gRPC  + Kafka for real -time ride tracking, fare calculation. •Amazon  → REST APIs for order services + event -driven SQS for inventory. •Banking  → Asynchronous messaging ensures transaction reliability. •Healthcare  → Event -driven updates (e.g., patient record changes notify multiple systems).

heading: Page 44
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TTechnology: Inter -micro services communication
Challenges in Inter -Service Communication
•Latency  → Multiple calls can slow responses. •Fault Tolerance  → One service failure can cascade. •Data Consistency  → Especially in asynchronous models. •Security  → Must authenticate and encrypt communications. Best Practices
•Use API Gateway  to manage external/internal requests. •Implement circuit breakers  (e.g., Hystrix ) for fault isolation. •Use service discovery  (e.g., Consul, Eureka) for locating services. •Use event -driven design  for scalability. •Secure communication with mTLS  + JWT .

Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TServerless Architecture
Serverless  computing  is a cloud -native  development  model  that allows  developers  to build  
and run applications  without  managing  servers . Serverless  Architecture  is a cloud -native  architecture  in which  the cloud  provider  
automatically  manages  the infrastructure,  while  developers  focus  only  on writing  
application  logic .

heading: Page 53
text:
•The cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP) automatically handles:
•Server provisioning
•Scaling
•Maintenance
•High availability
•Developers only write code  as functions , and the cloud takes care of the infrastructure. •Example
•AWS Lambda
•Azure Functions
•Google Cloud Functions

heading: Page 54
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TServerless Architecture
Key Characteristics
•No server management  → Servers exist, but abstracted away from developers. •Event -driven execution  → Functions trigger on events (HTTP request, file upload, DB 
change). •Pay-per-use → Billing is based on execution time and requests (not idle server time). •Scalable by default  → Functions auto -scale based on workload. •Stateless functions  → Each invocation is independent, no persistence in memory.

heading: Page 55
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TServerless Architecture
Serverless vs Traditional Architecture
Feature Traditional (Server -based) Serverless
Server Management Developer/DevOps manages Cloud provider manages
Scaling Manual / Auto -scaling setup Auto, on -demand
Billing Pay for uptime Pay per request/execution
Use Case Long -running apps Event -driven workloads

heading: Page 56
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TServerless Architecture
Building Blocks of Serverless
•FaaS  (Function as a Service)
•The heart of serverless. Developers write small, independent pieces of code 
(functions) that execute only when triggered by an event. •Example: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions. •Core idea: Write small independent functions → triggered by events. •Example: A Lambda function generates an OTP whenever a customer logs in. •BaaS (Backend as a Service)
•Ready -made cloud services that replace the need to build backend code for common 
tasks. •Cloud -hosted services used directly instead of writing backend code. •Example: Firebase Auth (authentication), AWS S3 (storage), DynamoDB (database). •Event Sources
•Events are the triggers  that make serverless functions run. •API Gateway, message queues, file uploads, IoT devices.

heading: Page 57
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TServerless Architecture
Workflow - How They Fit Together
•Event Source  triggers an action → e.g., user uploads an image. •FaaS  function  runs → e.g., function resizes the image. •BaaS service  stores or processes the result → e.g., resized image is saved in S3. So, Serverless = Event Sources + Functions ( FaaS ) + Cloud Services (BaaS
In serverless, functions ( FaaS ) are triggered by events and often use backend services (BaaS) 
to get work done.

heading: Page 57
text:
Advantages
•Faster development → focus only on code. •Lower cost → pay only for execution. •High scalability. •Simplified operations (no patching, no server monitoring).

heading: Page 58
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TServerless Architecture
Challenges / Limitations
•Cold start problem  → Delay in execution when function is idle for long. •Statelessness  → Functions can’t store session data locally. •Vendor lock -in → Hard to migrate between AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, etc. •Debugging complexity  → Harder compared to traditional apps. Real -Time Applications
•Chatbots  → Serverless functions respond to user queries (Amazon Lex + Lambda). •IoT Processing  → Devices send data to the cloud → processed by Lambda. •Image/Video Processing  → Upload image → function resizes/filters it. •Event Notifications  → Trigger emails/SMS when events occur.

heading: Page 58
text: •Data Pipelines  → Serverless functions clean and transform data before storage.

heading: Page 61
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TFunction as a service ( Faas )
Introduction
Function as a Service ( FaaS ) is a cloud computing model  where developers write individual 
functions  that run in response to events . •It is the core of serverless computing . •Examples: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions . Instead of managing whole applications or servers, you just deploy functions . Key Characteristics
•Event -driven execution  → Functions triggered by events (API call, file upload, DB change). •Short -lived & stateless  → Functions run for a short time, no memory between runs.

heading: Page 61
text: •Automatic scaling  → Scales up/down based on number of requests. •Pay-per-execution  → Only pay for the time function runs. •Cloud -managed  → Infrastructure, servers, and scaling are managed by provider.

heading: Page 62
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TFunction as a service ( Faas )
How FaaS  Works (Workflow)
1.Developer writes a function (e.g., processImage ). 2.Function is uploaded to cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP). 3.An event occurs (e.g., image upload, API request). 4.Cloud provider runs the function automatically. 5.Function completes, resources are released. Advantages
Cost -efficient  → Pay only when functions run. Faster development  → Focus only on business logic. High scalability  → Handles 1 request or 1 million requests.

heading: Page 62
text: No infrastructure management .

heading: Page 63
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TFunction as a service ( Faas )
Challenges
•Cold start latency  → Delay if function hasn’t run recently. •Stateless limitation  → No memory or session persistence. •Execution limits  → Functions usually have max execution time (e.g., AWS Lambda 15 
mins). •Vendor lock -in → Hard to move functions between AWS, Azure, GCP .

heading: Page 63
text:
Real -Time Applications of FaaS
•Image Processing  → Auto -resize or watermark images when uploaded to cloud storage. •Chatbots & Voice Assistants  → Functions triggered by user queries (e.g., Alexa Skills using 
AWS Lambda). •IoT Data Handling  → Sensors send data, functions process it in real time. •Notifications  → Auto -send SMS/Email when an event occurs.

heading: Page 63
text: •Data Transformation  → Clean and format data before sending to databases. •API Backend  → Create APIs without managing servers (using API Gateway + Lambda).

heading: Page 64

Aspect Microservices FaaS  (Function -as-a-Service)
DefinitionAn application is broken into independent services

demand in the cloud. Deployment 
UnitEach service is a containerized app  (runs 
continuously).Each function is a piece of code  deployed to the 
cloud provider. Execution 
ModelRuns 24/7  or until stopped. Always available.Event -driven : Executes only when triggered (e.g., API

Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TModelling: Functions
Introduction
•In cloud -native applications , complex systems are broken into smaller, independent 
units . •Functions  are the smallest deployable and executable unit of logic. •Instead of building huge monolithic applications, developers model business logic as 
functions . •
  This approach is event -driven, stateless, and cloud -managed .

heading: Page 69
text: Why Model as Functions? •Simplicity  → Focus only on “what function does,” not on infrastructure. •Reusability  → Same function can be used across services. •Scalability  → Functions scale independently. •Maintainability  → Easier debugging and updates. •Cost -efficiency  → Pay only when functions execute.

heading: Page 70
text:
Cloud Native Architecture for Modern Platforms - 21CSE477TModelling: Functions
Key Characteristics of Functions
•Stateless  → Each execution is independent, no memory of past runs. •Event -driven  → Triggered by external events (API call, file upload, DB update).

heading: Page 70
text:
•Single responsibility  → Each function does one thing well. •Composable  → Functions can be chained together to build workflows. •Cloud -Managed lifecycle  → Deployment, scaling, and monitoring handled by provider. Modeling Functions in Cloud -Native Systems
When designing a cloud -native app:
•Identify Events  → (user uploads file, IoT device sends data). •Define Functions  → (resize image, validate data, send notification). •Choose Triggers  → (HTTP request, database change, message queue). •Connect Functions  → Combine multiple functions to create workflows (using event buses 
or orchestrators). •Deploy Independently  → Each function can evolve separately.

Benefits of Function Modeling
•Faster innovation → Focus on logic, not infrastructure. •Easy to test small pieces. •Fault isolation → Failure in one function won’t crash entire system. •Encourages microservices mindset. Challenges
•Cold start delays  → May take time if function not recently used. •Stateless only  → Persistent data must be stored externally. •Complex orchestration  → Multiple functions require coordination. •Vendor lock -in → Hard to migrate functions between providers.

Orchestration vs. Choreography :
•Orchestration : Central controller decides flow (e.g., AWS Step Functions, Azure Logic

•Example: PaymentSuccess  event is published, Email service listens  and sends
